intro: A recipe is a set of promises. If you give it the right amounts, in the right order, at the right heat, it will give you the same food it gave the person who wrote it. Most of the time a recipe fails, the recipe kept its promise and the cook did not. The flour was scooped instead of spooned. The tablespoon was really a teaspoon. The butter was not softened because nobody read step one until step four. This unit is about keeping your end of the deal.

You will start with the tools: the nested dry cups, the clear liquid cup with its spout, the set of measuring spoons, and the kitchen scale that professional bakers trust over all of them. You will learn the equivalents chart until 3 teaspoons, 4 tablespoons and 2 cups are as automatic as four quarters to a dollar. You will measure the hard ingredients, butter, shortening, brown sugar and honey, so that the whole amount reaches the bowl every time.

Then you will read recipes the way cooks read them: the parts, the mixing words, the heat words, and the hidden time that ruins dinners. You will scale a recipe up for a crowd and down for two, converting units as you go and checking that your pot is big enough. And you will set up a lab the way a restaurant sets up a station, everything in its place, with a time plan that ends when the bell rings and not after.
bigQuestion: How does a cook turn a recipe on a card into the same good food, at any size, every time?

The Pure Food and Drug Act requires honest labels on food sold across state lines

words.d: a cup with a flat rim, filled to the top and leveled; comes in a nested set
a clear cup with a spout and lines on the side, read at eye level on a flat surface
the method for flour and other dry goods: spoon lightly into the cup, then sweep the top flat
an amount that equals another in a different unit, such as 3 tsp = 1 Tbsp or 4 cups = 1 quart
a measure of liquid volume; 8 fluid ounces make a cup
the scale button that resets the display to zero with a bowl on it
brown sugar pressed firmly into the cup until it holds the cup's shape when turned out
how much a recipe makes: servings, pieces or pans
the number every ingredient is multiplied by when scaling: servings wanted divided by servings the recipe makes
to combine gently with a spatula so a light mixture keeps its air
to cook in liquid just below a boil, with small slow bubbles
everything measured, prepped and set out before the heat goes on

test.q: Which tool is right for 3/4 cup of flour?
choices: The 3/4 cup dry measure, spooned and leveled
The liquid cup filled to the 3/4 line
A coffee mug three quarters full
test.why: Flour is a dry ingredient: dry cup, spooned in lightly, leveled with a straight edge.

test.q: How many tablespoons are in 1/4 cup?
Where should your eye be when reading 1 cup of milk in a glass measuring cup?
choices: Level with the line, with the cup on the counter
Anywhere, as long as you pour slowly
test.why: Reading at eye level on a flat surface shows the true level. Above or below shifts the reading.
A stick is 1/2 cup, 8 Tbsp, 4 oz, and the wrapper is marked in tablespoons.

test.q: A recipe calls for 1 lb of ground beef. What does 1 lb mean here?
choices: 16 ounces by weight, checked on a scale or the package label
16 fluid ounces, measured in a liquid cup
2 cups packed into a dry measure
test.why: Pounds are weight. 16 oz = 1 lb. Cups measure volume and do not apply.

test.q: A cake rose fast, sank in the middle, and tastes soapy. Which mistake fits?
choices: A heaping spoon of baking soda instead of a level one
Eggs beaten in one at a time
test.why: Too much leavening makes batter rise and collapse and leaves a soapy taste. Level every spoon.

test.q: Which ingredient is packed into the measuring cup on purpose?
test.why: Brown sugar is measured packed unless the recipe says otherwise. Everything else is spooned and leveled.

test.q: How many cups are in a quart?
test.why: 2 cups = 1 pint and 2 pints = 1 quart, so 4 cups make a quart.

test.q: A recipe serves 4. You need 12. What is the factor, and what happens to 1/2 tsp of salt?
test.why: 12 divided by 4 is 3. Every ingredient, including salt, is multiplied by 3: 1/2 tsp times 3 is 1 1/2 tsp.

test.q: After scaling, a recipe needs 20 cups of broth. How much is that in quarts?
test.why: 4 cups = 1 quart, so 20 cups is 5 quarts, a gallon plus a quart.

test.q: A recipe says cream the butter and sugar. What does that mean?
choices: Melt them together in a pan
Stir them for a few seconds with a spoon
Beat them together until pale and fluffy, 2 to 3 minutes
test.why: Creaming beats air into the fat, which makes cookies and cakes light. It takes a few minutes.

test.q: A soup should simmer. What does the pot look like?
choices: Bubbles only at the very edge of a cold pot
Small bubbles rising slowly and a barely moving surface
test.why: Simmering is just below a boil. A rolling boil is too hard for soups and breaks food apart.

test.q: Which is the correct order for starting a cooking lab?
choices: Read the recipe, wash hands 20 seconds, set out tools, measure everything, then turn on the heat
Turn on the heat, then measure, then read the recipe
Measure as you go with the pan already hot
Wash hands after cooking, before eating
test.why: Mise en place: everything read, washed, set out and measured before the heat goes on.

test.q: A 45-minute lab: cleanup takes 8 minutes and eating takes 5. By what minute must the food be ready to eat?
test.why: 45 minus 8 is 37; 37 minus 5 is 32. Backward planning starts from the end.

test.q: The recipe needs 1 cup buttermilk and you have only plain milk. What do you do?
choices: Use 1 cup of plain milk with nothing added
Put 1 Tbsp vinegar or lemon juice in the cup, fill to 1 cup with milk, wait 5 minutes
test.why: Buttermilk's job is to be sour so it reacts with baking soda. Milk plus an acid does the same job.

write.prompt: A cookie recipe makes 24 cookies and your class needs 60. Write the plan: find the factor, scale each ingredient and convert any awkward amounts into the easiest measure, then list the steps of your lab in order with a clock time for each, and explain why each step is where it is.
tips: Show the factor as a division problem (60 divided by 24) and multiply every line by it, including salt and leavening.
Use the equivalents chart: turn tablespoons into cups and teaspoons into tablespoons where you can.
Name the tool for each ingredient (dry cup, liquid cup, spoon, scale) and say how you fill it: spooned and leveled, packed, or read at eye level.
Plan backward from the end of the period, and say what you do while the cookies bake.
Check your numbers twice, and say how many pans you need so the batter is not deeper than the recipe planned.
